title: Fifth commandment: life and peace (CCC 2258–2317)
hookLine: respect for every life and the work of peace

cards: Two brothers, at the very start of the Bible's story. One farms, one keeps sheep. Both bring offerings; one is accepted, one isn't, and the older brother's face falls.
God warns him that sin is waiting at the door, and that he can master it. He doesn't listen. He invites his brother out into the field, and there he kills him.
Then God asks Cain where his brother is, and Cain shrugs: am I my brother's keeper? The fifth commandment begins in that field.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not kill." The Catechism begins with why. Human life is sacred, because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God and stays forever in a special relationship with him.

teach.h: LIFE IS SACRED: GOD ALONE IS ITS LORD.
teach.b: God alone is the Lord of life.
In the field, God tells Cain: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." Even a life no one else saw taken is heard. Then the Catechism walks through hard ground, carefully.
It allows legitimate self-defense, and the duty to protect those in one's care.

It teaches that life must be protected from conception, and it rejects euthanasia and suicide, while asking for prayer for those who have died by suicide and saying we should not despair of their salvation.
If thoughts of ending your life are close to you, you're not alone: please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Its current text calls the death penalty inadmissible.

And it warns about scandal: leading another person to do wrong. Then the commandment reaches inside. Jesus says whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment; violence starts in the heart.
So the section ends with peace, more than the absence of war.
It quotes Augustine, peace is the tranquility of order, and calls peace the work of justice and the effect of charity.

It lists strict conditions before any war could be called just, and asks everyone to work to avoid war. Cain asked if he was his brother's keeper. In Catholic teaching, the answer is yes: every life, and every peace.

how: Catholics examine themselves on the fifth commandment before confession, including anger and grudges; the sign of peace at Mass, shared before Communion, puts the commandment into a gesture.

games.q: you're Cain. your brother's offering was accepted and yours wasn't. God warns you that sin is waiting at the door. what do you do?
o: master it, and go do well.
invite your brother out into the field.
games.why: God tells Cain he can have dominion over sin. in Genesis 4, Cain doesn't: he takes his brother into the field and kills him.

practice: Let one person come to mind with whom something is unsettled: a cold silence, a sharp word, an old grudge. Picture their face without the argument attached, and ask what one small step toward peace would look like.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, wish them well, honestly, once.

wordCard.voice: Fifth commandment. Thou shalt not kill: respect for every human life, from beginning to end, and the daily work of peace, starting with anger. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the verb in Exodus 20:13, 'thou shalt not kill'.

carryVoice: Your line: every life. Peace starts where anger starts, on the inside. See you tomorrow.
